The house resumed from Monday, March 6, consideration in committee of Bill No. 40, respecting visiting forces of His Majesty, and the exercise of command, discipline and attachments of commonwealth forces when serving together-Mr. Bennett-Mr. Hanson (York-Sunbury) in the chair.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this bill
was partly proceeded with at the last sitting, during which the right hon. leader of the opposition raised certain questions which I indicated I would investigate in order to be in a position to answer at the next sitting. I have discussed these questions with the legal adviser of the Department of External Affairs in the interval. The only copy of the British bill in our possession is the one in the files, which I will now hand to the right hon. gentleman so that he may look it over. My information is that this bill has been passed, and that a bill in similar terms has been passed in South Africa as well. I observe from the debates in the British house that Sir Boyd Merriman, solicitor general, declined to make certain changes suggested because he said the bill had been agreed upon and had been enacted already in South Africa. In the House of Lords certain objections were taken as to the effect of the legislation being to deprive the British courts of jurisdiction which they had always asserted, but the House of Lords did not feel disposed to make the amendment suggested, and dt stands in the form in which it appears in this bill.
I think the observations made by the right hon. gentleman the other day as to the preamble are not wholly without some merit, and in order that there may be no misapprehension I propose to move in amendment that the title be struck out and that the title of the bill be:
An act to make provision with respect to forces of His Majesty from other parts of the British commonwealth or from a colony when visiting the Dominion of Canada; and with respect to the exercise of command and

Visiting Commonwealth Forces
discipline when forces of His Majesty from different parts of the commonwealth are serving together; and with respect to the attachment of members of one such force to another such force, and with respect to deserters from such forces.
I propose that this be made the long title of the bill, there being a short title within the statute itself, and that the preamble be eliminated.

What will be the short
title?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The short title is contained in section 1 of the bill; The Visiting Forces (British Commonwealth) Act, 1933. I think that meets the difficulty in that regard. Perhaps I might refer to the objections which were taken before we go on to consider them in detail. I think the objection taken as to the minister being the authority to take action is well founded; I believe that in a country such as this it is desirable that the governor in council rather than the minister should assume the responsibility, so I propose to move an amendment in that sense to the various sections of t'he bill in which the word occurs. Of course the next amendment that would take place would insert the words "His Majesty, by and with the advice and consent of the Senate and House of Commons of Canada enacts as follows:"
Mr. LAPOINTE; I am sorry I was not here when the matter was discussed previously, but would the Prime Minister say whether there is any change in the situation as it previously existed except that instead of being governed by an Imperial statute the matter will be dealt with by a Canadian statute? Will it be the same thing in effect as a result of this legislation or are there changes in the situation?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
There are a few minor
changes, with respect to visiting forces, dealing with points that were not adequately covered by any existing legislation, but the general principles of discipline, which as the hon. gentleman knows the provisions of the Army Act extended to every part of the empire, are adopted. This bill makes no change except that it makes clear beyond peradventure that the courts of this country would be the courts to which application for habeas corpus would be made in the event of any action being taken in consequence of a military decision. That position was challenged in the House of Lords, as I have said, and a discussion took place between Lord Hailsham, Lord Buckmaster and others, but in the end the section stood in the form in which it now appears.
There is one other matter to which I think attention should be directed. It was thought by the right hon. leader of the opposition the other day that possibly the last section effected some change in existing conditions. That is not intended, and I think in fact no change has been made. It became clear that the provisions of the act of 1911, which was passed by the Imperial parliament after the 1911 conference in connection with the government of naval forces, extended to every part of the empire, but of course it is competent for the parliament of any dominion to enact its own code. Until that is done, however, this act saves that power and makes it clear that there is no interference with the provisions of the statute as it stands.
I think those were the points to which attention was directed, and I would make the motion as to the cutting out of the preamble and making it part of the title of the bill, rather than an operative part of the act.
I would direct the right hon. gentleman's attention to rule 76, which provides that any change in the title of a bill must be taken up last.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I know, but this merely substitutes the preamble for the title.
Mr. MACKENZIE KING; I cannot see just what difference the change is going to make in,the actual effect of the bill. It seems to me that all the Prime Minister is doing is to give the bill the preamble as a name, and strike out the preamble.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: That is all.
So that we are really not changing the provisions in any particular.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: But the effect is considerable.
I want to make it clear that as to the actual provisions of the bill they will not be affected one way or the other.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: No.

The Prime Minister has indicated that he thinks it would be advisable to substitute "the governor in council" for "the Minister of Defence" with respect to certain powers given particularly, I believe, under section 6 of the bill. As I previously said, I believe that is a desirable change and I am glad the Prime Minister is of that view.

Visiting Commonwealth Forces

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: It is subsection 2 of section 6.

Yes. May I return now to the point I raised at the outset, which in effect was this. I gathered at the time the bill was introduced that the Prime Minister was of the opinion that it related solely to forces from other parts of the empire visiting Canada, and what should be done with respect to command and control while they were here. I pointed out at the time that I believed the bill went further and that it had relation as well to forces from Canada which might be in Great Britain and might be sought for service together with the forces of Great Britain or those of other parts of the empire, at a time of war; in other words, that the measure was a war as well as a peace measure. I still entertain that view. The difference at the moment is that whereas under the act as it now reads the Minister of National Defence in Canada would have power to place certain forces under a single command in Great Britain, if he so desired, that power, when the Prime Minister's amendment is accepted, will reside in the governor in council. I still think there is some slight risk being run in leaving that power even with the governor in council unless it is very clearly understood that the policy with respect to having forces of Canada serve abroad will be that they shall be placed for service abrpad only after this parliament has sanctioned their going abroad for the purpose of service. There is nothing in the law as it stands to-day which says that parliament must be convened in the first instance, but I think the Prime Minister made it clear that so far as he is concerned he would feel that parliament should be called in the first instance. There is nothing in this legislation, however, to necessitate that.
May I point out by way of a concrete instance exactly what I have in mind. In 1922 the government of this country was asked by the British government whether we would send a contingent to participate with the British forces in the near east in an effort to withstand aggression of the Turks upon Europe. The Liberal government of the day took the view that parliament should be called in the first instance and that its consent would have to be obtained before any forces should be permitted to go abroad to serve in conjunction with other military forces. We were criticized in some quarters for taking that view. We were told that instead of replying that parliament should be called in

the first instance and give its consent, we should have said "Ready, aye, ready" and placed our forces immediately at the disposition of the British government along with other British forces. If that "Ready, aye, ready" view were accepted there would be power under the legislation we are now enacting for the governor in council to place Canadian forces at the disposition of His Majesty's government in Great Britain and under a single command in Great Britain before the parliament of Canada might have any say in the matter at all.
That is the feature which I wished if possible to guard against, and to guard against in this legislation. There is apparently no difference of view between the Prime Minister and myself as to the desirability of calling parliament in the first instance, but I think it would strengthen the position with relation to subsequent parliaments if we made quite clear that parliament itself should decide in the first instance upon the disposition of Canadian forces, where that involves their being placed under single command for service in other parts of the empire or of the world.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I asked the legal adviser of the Department of External Affairs, without reference to myself, to prepare a statement of what he conceived to be the correct position of the matter from the point of view of a lawyer, after he had looked through the discussion at the last sitting, and perhaps the right hon. gentleman will let me read these words:
Mr. King was evidently under the impression that this clause enabled the Minister of National Defence to send a detachment from Canada in case of war. without the authority either of council or of parliament. The object of the clause is solely to make possible the interchange of officers and other ranks that has been the practice for many years. Legally, it would not authorize the sending of a detachment, and it would not authorize the sending of individuals to become a detachment or unit after they had gone to the other part of the commonwealth. The object of the clause, together with the following subsection is to enable an officer from the United Kingdom, when on temporary service in Canada, to carry on his duties. Without this section, it would be necessary to recommission him; otherwise, if he gave an order to a subordinate officer or other rank, there -would be no legal obligation to obey the order.
It is quite clear that you would have to send a number of individuals, sufficient to constitute a detachment to be attached to the force abroad, to meet the case which the right hon. gentleman suggests. This statute is prepared for one purpose -and one purpose only; that is, to enable individuals that are

Visiting Commonwealth Forces
attached to the forces of the United Kingdom or of one of the other dominions to be properly governed without being re-commissioned. That was the understanding I had of the matter, but I felt there might be some doubt and I asked for a memorandum. I make this statement to the right hon. gentleman as frankly as possible because the legal adviser was of the opinion that it would not be possible for them to become a detachment after they had gone. He says:
It would not authorize the sending of individuals to become a detachment or unit after they had gone to the other part of the commonwealth.
Further, he makes this statement:
In one sense it is true to say that the provision would govern war conditions. When forces are cooperating in time of war, it is necessary to make temporary attachments occasionally. For example, I remember when I was serving in France, an English officer was attached for instructional purposes to our battery. Without such a provision, it would be legally impossible for an officer in his position to carry on during his temporary period of attachment.
I think that is reasonably clear. If the statute were one not agreed upon there might be some reason why the language might be clarified, were there any doubt about it. But I put this to the right hon. gentleman. It is quite clear that under no circumstances, as the law now stands, could we dispatch from this country any substantial number of men if we desired to do so because, as I have said, the statute now calls for parliament to meet in fifteen days after the country is at war, and I certainly agree that it would be impossible to send from this country any substantial number of troops under the appropriations as we now have them, without a governor general's warrant; and I cannot conceive of a government asking for a warrant and calling parliament together, as it must, within fifteen days from the date of hostilities or declaration of war. So that I do not think there is the slightest danger of any difficulty arising from the passing of this statute or in connection with its provisions. But in view of our commitments in 1929, followed by the resolutions of 1930 and the agreement arrived at with respect to the statute in the present form, I can only say that in my opinion we are in honour bound to enact the measure as they have done in South Africa and the United Kingdom. If there is the slightest likelihood of any difficulty, such as that to which the right hon. genleman has alluded, we can take the appropriate steps to provide against it. I would hesitate to accept the responsibility of making any substantial amendment to what has been agreed upon.
The reasons are so apparent that it is almost unnecessary to state them. Sir Boyd Merri-man made it clear in the British House of Commons that he could not take the responsibility of making an amendment to what had been agreed upon and enacted by one of the commonwealth parliaments, namely, that of South Africa. I regret that there is not a copy of the South African bill available. The only bill I have is the one I have just handed to the right hon. gentleman which is similar in terms, subject to the changes which had to be made as compared with the provisions governing the United Kingdom.

What the
Prime Minister has said serves to meet ir large part what I have in mind. I have nc desire to embarrass the administration with respect to any obligation they may have with any other government of the empire, but I do want to safeguard against any unforeseen contingency which may arise sometime hence.
I have in mind the Chanak incident which arose in 1922 when New Zealand and Australia were asked if they would place their naval sendees at the disposition of the empire in the near east. Before we in Canada even received the invitation from the government of Great Britain to participate in that particular matter, it was announced that the governments of New Zealand and Australia, either or both, I don't remember which, had placed their naval services at the disposition of the British government. Had we agreed to do the same, who can say what might have resulted? Canada's action steadied the situation. My feeling is that under this legislation power will be vested in the governor in council to place, for example, our naval services at the disposition of the British government and that for sometime before parliament can meet. It might well be that a regiment such as the Princess Patricia Canadian Light Infantry could be dispatched and sent overseas to be placed under a single command in Britain or in some other part of the empire before parliament could meet. From what the Prime Minister has said and from the legal opinion he has quoted, I know that such is not the object of this legislation, but nevertheless, this statute might provide the means whereby at some future time in a moment of excitement an object of that kind could be served. Having brought out this point, and having received such an emphatic and clear declaration from the Prime Minister as to the purpose of the bill, I need, perhaps, not say anything further.

Do the words "may be prescribed by regulations made by His Majesty" mean His Majesty as advised by the government of Great Britain, by the government of Canada or by the government in the part' of the empire in which the forces may be?

speechtext: Hon. W.A. GORDON (Minister of Labour) moved the second reading of Bill No. 55, respecting relief measures. '

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE YEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the house has discussed the provisions of this measure at such length on the resolution that preceded it that I shall not take up more than a few minutes in restating our position with respect to the principle involved as we are considering it on the second reading. In a word1, we are opposed to the measure now before us because in our opinion it is the negation of government by parliament. It is that in its two outstanding particulars. In the first place, it gives to the administration a blank cheque, the right to draw out of the consolidated fund of Canada unlimited amounts of money for any purpose whatever so long as the purpose may be said to be that of assisting in the relief of unemployment. As to how widely that power may be used, we

Relief Act, 1933-Mr. Mackenzie King
had evidence yesterday after the speech of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes) in listening to the interpretation placed by the administration upon the provisions of this bill in reference thereto. In introducing his budget, the Minister of Finance stated that there was to be created a stabilization fund in connection with certain agricultural products. It really is in the nature of a provision to subsidize the export of certain commodities from Canada to Great Britain. One would have felt that if such were the policy of the administration, the government, proceeding in the regular manner, would have brought in a bill for that purpose and made provision therefor, but we were told that the provision for that particular purpose was to be found in mone3rs that were being voted for purposes of unemployment relief. That certainly is not in accordance with parliamentary practice, nor is it constitutionally right. I do not see how we can approve the principle of a measure which permits a government to go that length. If a step of that kind can be taken with respect to subsidies, in matters of trade, it can be taken for almost any purpose for which the government may wish to use it. It will be seen that in such cases there is no control by parliament in any way over expenditure.
It has been shown also that when the government had this power before, it placed orders for a million and some odd dollars worth of railway ties which were not required by -the railways, and that this amount was charged up to the relief of the unemployed, although as a matter of fact the unemployed came in for a very small proportion of the money spent in that way. To give to the government that unlimited* power jn the use of public moneys is simply to help create debts which it will take years and years for this country to meet. I think people have discovered by the proposals brought down in yesterday's budget that they are going to have to pay pretty heavily for expenditures being made at this time. The increased taxes are going to hit the average citizen throughout Canada fairly hard. That is something which the people at the moment are feeling very keenly. But they should realize that every time this parliament parts with its control over expenditures and gives the government the right to draw whatever moneys it pleases out of the exchequer on blanket authority, they are only helping to place a greater burden upon themselves with respect to taxation. In our desire to limit taxation as much as possible, we feel that we should very strongly maintain the control which ordinary parliamentary procedure would 
demand in these matters, and oppose whatever destroys that control.
In saying what I do may I again make perfectly clear that we on this side are prepared, as we have been all along, to vote for purposes of unemployment relief whatever moneys the ministry may decide to be necessary, so long as those amounts are named, their purposes specified and some substantial reason for what is proposed given to the house. So our objection to the second reading is in no way based on a desire not to do all that may be possible to cooperate with the government in a regular manner in providing what funds may be necessary for unemployment relief.
Our second objection to the measure, and it is one that has arisen since the resolution was originally introduced, comes out of the amendment made when the resolution was before the house in committee, the amendment giving to the government of the day power by order in council to legislate with respect to peace, order and good government. As has been stated over and over again, an authority as broad as that enables the government to legislate simply by act of the governor in council on almost anything at all upon which it may wish to legislate. When the British North America Act was passed, the power to legislate was placed not in the executive nor in the judiciary, but in parliament as represented1 by this House of Commons and the Senate and His Majesty's representative in this country, and we cannot for one minute countenance the transference of that power from parliament to the governor in council as is proposed to be done under this measure.
May I add that, in the light of the discussion that has taken place on the measure, there is a further reason why we should not countenance it. It has been stated from this side, and I think hon. members of the house as a whole believe, that the government has under the statutes as they exist to-day all the power that it needs to deal with any situation that may arise. The provisions in this bill itself are very broad. They give to the government all the power that is needed certainly to deal wuth any questions of unemployment; they give all the power that is necessary to deal with any emergency in the nature of a financial crisis or panic, or even an insurrection, and that being so we see no reason why the government should seek this further authority of the right to enact notwithstanding all existing legislation, whatever measures it pleases by order in council so long as that legislation may be designated

Relief Act, 1933-Division
as coming under the heading of peace, order and good government.
Objecting to the measure on both those scores, the blank cheque, on the one hand, and the blanket authority to legislate, on the other, we feel that this measure, as I have said, is the negation of government by parliament, and as such we are strongly opposed to the second reading of the bill.

speechtext:
The hon. Minister of
Labour (Mr. Gordon) professed to be surprised the other day about certain facts that I submitted to the house. I quoted opinions expressed by His Excellency Monseigneur Ross, Bishop of Gaspe, by His Excellency Monseigneur Lapointe, honorary vicar-general of Chicoutimi, and by leaders of the church and state. What I said was what has also been said by many people. They were humble suggestions offered to the house and to the country with regard to colonization. The hon. gentleman told me that I had made an impeachment against my own province, the province of Quebec, which I love, and my hon. friend from Bellechasse (Mr. Boulanger) asked me for more details. I have given ample notice and warning of what I intend to do. I did so on March 2 when I spoke of generalities. I did so last Monday, going a little more thoroughly into the matter, but to-day at the request of the Minister of Labour and my hon. friend from Bellechasse I will give more precise details. I will ask my hon. friend the Minister of Labour to listen to what I am going to say, and I am very sorry that the hon. Minister of Pensions and National Health (Mr. Mac-Laren) is not in the house at the present time. I will tell you something about la Riviere Solitaire-and mark you, Mr. Chairman, I am not speaking against my own province, I am speaking on behalf of my own province and on behalf of my own fellow citizens who are there in the midst of the wilderness and whom 1 wish to defend in this house. I do not oare about the insinu-

Reliej Act, 1933
ations that may be made against me concerning it by any one in this house.
This week there appeared in Le Devoir, of Montreal, an article signed by Mr. Rioux, the president of the Catholic Union of Farmers of the province of Quebec, mentioning the fact that the Riviere Solitaire is twenty miles from the railway. And may I take this opportunity to thank the press of my country, and all the dailies and weeklies, especially the great and well-known daily of Montreal, La Presse, which published an excellent three column report of my speech of Monday last. The attention of the public should be drawn to a subject which is of the utmost importance for all this country. My hon. friend the Minister of Labour should know more about Riviere Solitaire because it is hundreds of miles from Riviere du Loup but only about eighty miles northeast of Haileybury. It is on the Perrault highway, a good road in the summer time but in winter time inaccessible. Since September last 2,800 settlers, I mean men, women and children, have been living there. Some have settled along the highways; others are some distance from the highways with no roads leading to their camps. They must travel over stumps and through the trees and bush, and many of those people have no means of locomotion. They receive $600 in all, $200 from the federal government, $200 from the provincial government and $200 from the municipality. In most cases that amount has been nearly all spent for travelling expenses and for the construction of camps and so on; almost nothing is left now. These people are wondering how they are to live when this $600 is all gone.
These families are about twenty miles from Rouyn. In that town there are some doctors who are employed by the mining companies, but in this settlement there is no doctor and only one nurse, a young woman. She is full of heroism and devotion to the people; she looks after them as best she can in that vast area. It is very hard there for a young woman; in the winter time she has to travel in a covered wagon in which there is a stove, and she must go many miles in order to help those who are in need. There has been an epidemic of itch. The heads of those families in the main are young people of from twenty-five to forty, and there is the question of children. I believe some sixty or eighty babies are expected by the middle of April, and who is to take care of them? No doctor from Rouyn can go there, so it all depends on one young girl. I am sorry to see that the minister is laughing. I am not laughing at all; I am very serious. The minister has
a good heart; he knows that I am not making these remarks for any personal reason. I am interested in the health and welfare of these people. This settlement is not far from where the minister lives, and he can verify what I say.
These families are away in the midst of a wilderness, and I say it would have been much more sensible if they had been placed on the farms which are for sale in the old parishes. In the second place I submit that a medical attendant should be sent there at once. If a man takes the risk of a long aeroplane journey and loses his way the papers are full of it and no government refuses to spend hundreds and perhaps thousands of dollars to search for him. Only one human life is concerned in that case, but here we are considering hundreds of human lives that are endangered. Those camps are surrounded now by snow and in the spring there will be slush and mud, and these people will not be able to leave the camps. The melting snow and ice and mud surrounding them will be a source of contamination and disease, and when that has dried up they will be exposed to forest fires. If there should be a fire after the snow goes, those men, women and children would all be burned to death just as those poor girls were burned in Hull some days ago. I do not wish to cast any slur upon anyone; I am discussing this matter because I want someone to go at once to the rescue of those people. They are entitled to medical attention. Certainly if the Minister of Labour has listened to my remarks, if the Minister of Health reads Hansard to-morrow and if the Minister of Colonization of Quebec sees what I have said they must agree that a government that can spend so much money to look after those who take the risk of long aeroplane trips can afford to spend a tew hundred dollars each month in order that these people may receive the medical attention and care to which they are entitled. I say it is a mistake that this has not been done. If the work had been in charge of a private organization that organization would have provided a doctor to look after that large number of people. That is done by the lumber companies, who employ only men, but here we have a situation much more serious because it involves women and children as well. I think it is time something was done in this regard. I hope the minister will take what I have said into consideration and that he will not dare suggest that my remarks in this house on behalf of my own people are an impeachment against my own province.
Relief Act, 1933

speechtext: I am sure the committee now understands that the administration and the selection of the locations where these colonists are settled is entirely under the control of the province. There is a committee upon which the Canadian National Railways, in the section to which reference has been made, is represented by Mr. Laforce, who acts under Doctor W. J. Black. I do know very well the section of country to which the hon. member for Temiscouata has made reference; I do not say this by way of complaint, but I am sure the hon. member has never been anywhere near that district or he could not have made the statements he has made.

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE YEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext:
I would say that I know
it better than the minister does.

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE YEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext:
Perhaps so, but my hon.
friend would have to know it very well indeed. In order that the observations of the hon. member for Temiscouata may not go abroad unchallenged and bring about fears and anxieties which I do not think should result from the efforts that have been made I must take the time of the committee to read the report made by Mr. Laforce on this very locality to which reference has been made. I will hurry through this report as rapidly as possible. It is directed to Doctor W. J. Black, Canadian National Railways, Montreal, under date of March 10, 1933, and is as follows:
As requested, I am giving you a summary report of the activities of the back to the land movement in the province of Quebec during the year 1932. During the year 523 families were accepted by the committee, and have been established mostly in Temiskaming and Abitibi listricts. The selection of these families was eonducted with as much care as was possible. After interviewing the future settlers, recommendations were requested from parish priests, religious ministers, aldermen of the wards in which the settlers resided, and from charitable institutions or associations which were assisting them.	'
This information was then submitted to the municipal council and afterwards to the back to the land committee. A few errors may have been made, but very few.
Each group of settlers was accompanied in order that they might not meet with difficulty. The family heads-
Rememlber tlhat the heads of families, the fathers, preceded the women and children.
-who went to Abitibi, for example, upon reaching Amos-
Amos is on the Canadian National Railways in Quebec.
-were received by Mr. V. Villeneuve, escorted to an "accommodation house" where they spent the night, and the following morning were conducted to the settlement where they chose their lots. Generally about two days after their
[Mr. It nil lot. j
arrival they were starting to build a temporary shelter which permitted them to remain on the lots whilst putting up their camp. These camps were mostly budt of logs, squared inside.
To hon. gentlemen who have no experience of pioneer colonization in this part of northern Canada I may explain that a house of logs is the first bouse which the settler invariably builds where timber is so plentiful.
It was understood that the floors were to be made of planed planks, tongued and grooved. The house was te be fitted with windows in order that it may be well lighted, and was to be one and one-half stories high, with room in the top part. The necessary lumber for floors and roof was brought to a central place where a general store also was put up, the operation of which is under the effective supervision of the government.
That is the Quebec government.
After the houses or camps were constructed, and then only, the families left for their new homes. Special cars (colonists) were placed at the disposal of these families. These cars were well ventilated, and all precautions were taken to see that the families met with the least possible difficulties. Each group was accompanied. On their arrival in Abitibi the families would get off the Canadian National Railway train and get on another train made of small houses on sleighs which were drawn by a tractor. Eighty persons could sit in two of these houses and be comfortable. On a third sleigh was the baggage, and then this new train left for the colony. These houses on sleighs were well lighted, supplied with fresh water, hammocks had been set up to permit the babies to sleep, and even a toilet room had been fitted out.
As you see the persons were treated with care. Land of the highest quality was selected for them in districts where the clearing is rather easy, not far from the railroad; another advantage offered in the districts where settlers were established in Abitibi is their proximity to the mining centres. The demands from these enterprises will supply the settlers w-ith a ready market for all they are able to grow.
One of the factors that contributed most to the success of the back to the land movement in Quebec in 1932 was that in each of the colonies a minister of the religion actively occupied himself to assist the settlers, to encourage them, and direct them.
To demonstrate how well satisfied the settlers are, permit me to give you below extracts from some of the letters we have received from new settlers of the district.
Perhaps it is unwise to give the names of these people settled on these lands, but I presume that those who write these letters would not object. I may add that these people are settled in communities and not scattered here and there through the wilderness.
Mr. Joseph Pichette, for example, who has selected a lot in the Villemontel township, writing to his brother, states:	"If X have
delayed writing to you it is because we have had much work to do. We have built our

Relief Act, 1933
camp, and everything goes well. I have a very nice piece of land, good soil, easy to clear. I am happy and satisfied with my lot, and so are the others."
Mrs. Paquin (a widow) writes to her daughter in the following terms: "Here everything goes smoothly. We are 'well treated, but we must take care not to squander, and work with intelligence. We cannot ask for anything better. Those who are criticizing would like us to be treated as though we were rich, and doing nothing. We have everything we need."
Another, Mr. Wilfrid Richard, who settled at LaMotte, writes us as follows: "I assure you that we are happy. My camp is 24 x 25 inside, with 7 rooms, li storeys high. While I am writing you my son is making a cupboard. We have put up a little stable 12 feet square, temporarily for this winter. My son in law, Raoul Robidoux (another back to the lander) is living with us. He is well satisfied and much encouraged."
Mr. Ephrem Larivieres, located in the Ville-montel township, states: "I have a very fine lot and am satisfied with my present situation. We have been well treated and those who, through newspapers or elsewhere are complaining. are wrong." He adds: "They are shamelessly lying."
Mrs. Jean Gaumont, of Villemontel. writing to a relative, expresses herself as follows: "I am very happy. I have made a beautiful trip; we made a joyous voyage, and still more happy to be here. You should see how nice it is. My husband has a good lot. He has put up a log camp, the joints of which have been packed with straw and moss.
That is the usual method of ehinking-up a log cabin.
These things are so new to me that I spend my time laughing. I like it so much that I would not return to Montreal."
Mr. Joseph Bellemare. who in the name of a group of fourteen families who have selected the district of Authier to establish themselves, writes to us under date of December 28, stating: "I wish to thank you most sincerely in my own name and that of the group, for sending us to such a good country."
Another settler of Villemontel, Mr. Joseph Dulude, writes:	"I have had all the time
necessity to look over the district and take information. From my little inquest I have come to the conclusion that in my case, and the experience I have with things of the land, being a farmer's son, I have every reason to believe that here I will succeed."
Mr. Joseph Lamothe, on January 29, writes: "I am writing these few words to let you know how we are, as well as my father in law, Mr. Ed. MeCrea (another back to the lander). I want to tell you that we are all very satisfied to be in Abitibi. . . ."
Mr. Joseph Lambert, on December 12, wrote the following: "Just a few lines to let you know we are getting settled in our new home fine, with which my wife and I are very much satisfied. Both my wife and I sincerely thank you for your trouble in getting us settled on a good farm on the highway, which we believe in a few years will mean good to us."
From the same place, Mr. Euge Therrien, veteran, writes:	"To my knowledge all the
settlers in the double range VI-VII are in perfect health and everyone has completed his 53719-210
camp, and to my information are all well satisfied with their lots, and as to myself I thank you gratefully."
Mr. Joseph Gingras writes: "We are very happy to be here, nobody is lonesome, and I can assure you, as far as I am concerned, it is the best move I have made in coming here. I have a very nice lot, half made, fire burnt everything.
He means the bush fires.
I have about twenty-five acres cleared around my camp, ready for seeding in the spring. I built a good camp. We call it a camp, but it is more like a house. I built 25 feet long by 22 feet wide, with a pointed roof, which makes two storeys. I made four rooms upstairs and two downstairs. We are better lodged than we were in Montreal. I dug a cellar, deep enough to walk in. I am two miles from the general store, it is not far, and when the church is constructed it will be near there. The road to the mines also passes that point. I am very confident that within a short while, without being very rich, we will be in a position to live without anxiety for the future."
Mr. Auguste Barbotin on the 18th of January writes: "We are all well satisfied with being here. We have had our first mission service this morning in front of my camp. It was very impressing." This Mr. Barbotin also wrote to the Travellers' Association, expressing his satisfaction, which letter waa published in the newspaper "Le Devoir."
From another district where families were established, Belcourt, Mr. Ferdinand Lupien declares, in a letter, that he is much pleased with his present situation. Other settlers from the same district also wrote to us thanking us for what we did for them.
Mr. A. Gagnon, from Uniacke, wrote us on the. 18th of January: "I left Montreal on the 3rd of October to come to Uniacke to establish myself on a colonization lot as settler, and with the idea of remaining here. I cannot let this occasion go by that presents itself to me to-day without taking advantage of it, and from the bottom of my heart offer you my sincere thanks, feeling that if I am here to-day I must be thankful to you. . .
Mr. Joseph Camirand, of Villemontel also, wrote to the St. Vincent de Paul Society to thank them, in which letter he says: ". . . have arrived safely and have put up my camp. I am very much satisfied with my lot and hope it will never' be necessary for me to go back to the city of Montreal."
Everyone of these persons left during last fall to settle in Abitibi and declare they are satisfied, not only with the manner in which they have been treated by the C.N.R., but also of the way in which they have been treated since settlement, because they have been given first class land, and care was taken for their establishment in a good district.
J. E. Laforce,
General Agent.
These reports are indicative of those we have received from the committee and the other agencies which are working, not to solve unemployment but to offer an opportunity to people who are ready, willing and able to place themselves or be placed in a position where they may be self-sustaining.

Hon. members will recall that not so many years ago Mr. David Lloyd George stated that the land was not playing the part it should at that time, and not so many days ago the President of the United States made reference to the same thing. I feel sure that the hon. member for Temiscouata has not made the investigation he should of the work carried on under the joint auspices of the agencies to which I have referred. I do not charge him for one moment with making statements which he knows are not founded upon fact but I feel sure that he has obtained his information from sources which might be almost looked upon with anxiety.

But the case is entirely different with those who have been placed away in the wilderness. I notice that most of the letters read were written just after these people had left the Canadian National agents.

speechtext: The descriptions they gave of their locations would indicate that they are from both sections. Being twenty miles from a railway is not an impossible situation for a settler. I know of settlers who opened up the Timiskaming district in Ontario who are to-day prosperous farmers and iff full ownership of their locations. Many of these settlers had to carry their provisions upon their backs for over thirty miles, and they did it without complaining. In spite of present conditions these men are very prosperous. With respect to the reference made to women having to ride in covered sleighs containing a stove, I may say that I have done that hundreds of times and I found it quite comfortable. In fact, I have ridden in open sleighs when it was fifty below zero, and I did not freeze to death.

speechtext:
I submit that reports received from the employees of the government should be received with a grain of salt. The employees in the colonization departments of

the Canadian Pacific or Canadian National have to show results in order to retain their jobs when reductions in staff are made. I think the minister should be careful in accepting the statements of such employees. They have to show results and those results are not based upon the selecting of settlers but rather upon the number of settlers placed upon the land, whether or not they possess the necessary qualifications. I have no ulterior motive in bringing up this matter, I did it because I thought it to be my duty. Unpleasant things may be said to me but I do not care. I am doing what my conscience tells me I should do and what I have done has been done as a representative of the people of Canada. Should similar circumstances arise in the future I shall follow a similar course.

speechtext:
The minister will remember that last year I took .objection to the methods adopted in the spending of federal money for unemployment relief in the province of New Brunswick. I instanced a case where the federal government had been committed to an expenditure of some $57,000 for the construction of a power line. I claimed that that was a revenue producing enterprise controlled by the power commission of the province, and therefore the Dominion government money should not be used. Not only was it a revenue producing enterprise, it was a profit producing enterprise. The province of New Brunswick was well able to build the line under the direction of the power commission and thus provide employment for the unemployed.
I have another complaint to register this year, and I should like the minister to give his strict attention. I think it was in 1928 that the legislature of the province of New Brunswick passed an act granting a bonus to farmers who cleared more acres of lancl than they had previously under cultivation. I think, Mr. Chairman,
that perhaps the hon. member is not fair to the Minister of Labour in presenting the case as he has done. The fact is that for many years, under t'he ordinary system followed in British Columbia, the provincial government has made certain grants out of provincial taxes to municipalities-grants to hospitals, grants towards education and matters of that kind. In more recent years, since government control of liquor has come in, there has been a share of the profits from liquor distributed amongst the municipalities upon the basis of the amount of liquor sold within the municipality, and other matters of that kind. But what this committee must bear in mind is

Relief Act, 1933
that that is purely a local, ordinary situation, and has nothing to do with relief. It has no relation to relief whatever.
It is quite true that British Columbia, in common with other provinces, the western provinces perhaps more so than parts of eastern Canada, has been confronted with difficult problems in connection with relief. No one questions that at all, and no one other than a person who was completely indifferent to local conditions could do otherwise than feel more or less perturbed about this problem. But it is not fair to say that the province of British Columbia is bankrupt or that the government of British Columbia is wholly indifferent. It is neither fair nor correct to make statements of that kind. The province of British Columbia is not bankrupt. At the same time unquestionably, like many other governments, the government of British Columbia is finding it very difficult to make ends meet with its depleted revenues, and this is not to be wondered at in a province like British Columbia where in years gone by one of the main sources of revenue was the returns from the timber trade, royalties on timber and so forth. Those royalties have fallen off as well as royalties on every other natural resource, and there is no question that the revenues of the province have been very seriously depleted. Nor would I or anyone else hesitate to say that., in the past, in British Columbia, as in all other places, the present government and other governments, have been perhaps unduly extravagant, or to put it in the kindest way, have been perhaps overoptimistic, and expenditures have run into very large figures. But that does not concern this committee dealing with a relief bill. What this committee is concerned about is this:	In its administration of the Relief Act
is this government dealing reasonably fair with the province of British Columbia as compared with other provinces? That I think is a fair subject for debate. I am quite certain from what I have bean able to gather from the Department of Labour and the minister that British Columbia has been equitably and reasonably well treated in the matter of relief.
May I take this opportunity of pointing out to 'the committee this fact, and I do it with great earnestness because personally I feel very much perturbed over it. It is this, that there is altogether too much tendency for our people in Canada, starting with the individual and going on up to the municipality and then the province, to lean too heavily upon governments. It is not necessary to blame people or denounce them for that, but the fact is there. Over a period of time we have grown
into the habit of leaning upon governments. The individual in the smaller localities has been looking for the municipality to provide all the relief he requires, without perhaps making that degree of individual effort which would contribute measurably towards his own relief; and the municipality has the tendency to lean entirely upon the provincial authorities, and so with the provincial authorities the tendency has been to pass the responsibility to Ottawa. That is something for which we cannot blame this man or that man; it is very common. But it is the duty of the Minister of Labour, as the minister responsible and charged with this very, very difficult task, to resist in a measure at least simply passing the responsibility up to him. What he has done, and I think done admirably, in the last three years of very trying times, has 'been so to direct the appropriations for relief from this government that there will be a maximum of returns. I think that he and the rest of us who are associated with him would be quite ready to admit that in handling this new situation which was thrust upon us errors have been made. I have no doubt that if we were to start all over again, faced with the situation of three years ago, we would find things that we might have done better. But that is only human, and hon. gentlemen .opposite, while quite within their rights and within their duty in criticizing the government, I am quite certain would at least recognize that necessarily there must have been some errors made. But I do submit, and I am speaking now about British Columbia about which I know a good deal, that the minister and his department have treated that province with very, very great consideration, and he and the rest of us who assist him from time to time in studying these matters, are pretty well alive to the needs. At the same time it would be mere folly for him to give way at once when any municipality wires or writes in, as they do frequently to myself, as the minister representing that province, seeking direct contaots. It would be very foolish to give way to appeals of that kind.
I do not apprehend any very serious disturbances from this new situation which has arisen in the province. As the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill) has said, there are certain persons, commonly known as the red element, who work amongst the unemployed and those ,on relief, capitalizing their distress and urging them on to deeds of violence. While we know there is a certain amount of that, I have sufficient knowledge of the sound common sense of the bulk of the people of British Columbia, unemployed or
Relief Act, 1933

employed, on relief or not on relief, to be confident that there will be no very great difficulty in that regard. There may be, is bound to be some, I presume; there has been in the past. But I notice that these disturbances that are foretold with great foreboding often do not amount to anything very serious. This we can say with confidence, that the members of the provincial government having to do with this matter-Hon. Mr. Bruhn, Hon. Mr. Jones, Hon. Mr. MacKenzie and others- are making strenuous efforts to deal with their local problem. Undoubtedly they are meeting with difficulties, but they are doing a great deal more in the way of effective work than I think is generally realized. I know from my own personal contacts with the Minister of Labour here, that the federal department responds to the appeals that are constantly being made-not immediately giving what is asked, because that would be sheer folly; but making a generous response in the way of funds, taking a sympathetic attitude toward the problems involved, and seeking by combined effort and joint knowledge of the situation to work out their solution. I would say to my hon. friend from Comox-Alberni that the minister would be ill-advised to take up appeals from individual municipalities. If he does that; if he abandons the principle we have followed of dealing with this matter through the provincial authorities, he will be called upon to establish duplicate organizations here and there throughout British Columbia; and if he did it there he would have to do it elsewhere. And I am reminded that the act itself, and all our powers hitherto asked for, provide only for dealing with provinces. I submit in all earnestness that it would be shear folly for this house to authorize the minister to deal with municipalities, cities or localities; it would entail the erection of an organization that would simply duplicate that of the provinces. I suggest to the hon. gentleman who put this forward, and to other hon. gentlemen speaking for British Columbia, that we should endeavour as far as we can to impress upon those in authority in the municipalities, as well as upon private citizens, that they must bear a larger share, not so much of the cost but of the effort to solve the problems with which we are from time to time confronted. I feel very strongly that if the people of Canada-we were speaking of British Columbia, but it can be made general-would realize that, and give a larger measure of personal effort to a solution of the difficulties, much better progress would be made.

But in order that the position may be made very plain let me remind the committee that rightly or wrongly the government has hitherto placed no limit upon what shall be spent in any province of this dominion for direct relief. We promptly pay the bills, after looking them over to see so far as possible that the moneys are not spent improperly, and that applies to British Columbia as well as to every other province. I receive communications from various provinces in regard to the situation in various districts and consideration is given to all submissions that are made. This also applies equally to British Columbia. I have heard a good deal about the possible looting of stores in certain sections of Canada, but on inquiry of the provincial authorities I have found that they had the matter in hand. I am not going to urge upon a province that they have not the matter in hand, that they should do this or do that within their legislative competence; I do not think any member of the committee would suggest that I should do so.
Let me say, however, that as these matters arise I am aware that there is an acute situation here or there within Canada, and if it is a question of providing funds we do confer with the provinces and take such action as is necessary to relieve such situations. But I

cannot too strongly urge that there is an agitation-I do not know how great it is in this country-absolutely to refuse to do any useful work. Some people seem to have made it their objective in life to wreck everything, and the refusal to do anything is one method of accomplishing that end. That is a difficult class of people to handle. Fortunately I believe it is a very small class, but there are many people in this country who are trying their utmost to improve their position. If we were to lay down a rule that in a certain province we would give so much per month to a family of two, so much to a family of three, and so on, in my view that would not be a proper course to adopt. It is human nature not to persist in trying to go upstream; it is such a comfortable thing to go down with the current. If people are taught to believe that the rather indefinable institution called the- state can take up the slack, no matter how great it may be, which may come about by reason of misadventure or the desire of the individual not to exert himself, then things will have come to a pretty pass indeed. It is part of my duty as Minister of Labour administering this act to see on the one hand that injustice and suffering shall hot prevail and on the other hand that the malingerer is not permitted to follow that course if measures can be adopted that will prevent him. This is not an easy act to administer, but I can assure the members of the committee that so far as it is humanly possible the course I have ind;-^ cated is being followed. I am sure hon. members know from their personal interviews with me in connection with matters in their particular ridings that the department is doing everything possible to endeavour to make the position of the worthy Canadian as easy as possible until better times come.

We have been told again and again about the prosperity which is coming to us but which has not yet come, and we are still exhorted to wait patiently .a few weeks or a few months longer, when the promised prosperity will come. There is no indication immediately in sight of anything of the kind and it is not unreasonable therefore for us to ask the government to face this question fairly with regard to the continuance
in considerable part of this unemployment situation. This they are not doing at the present time.
The minister told us the other night that one of the reasons why it was not wise for the state to do anything was that possibly the springs of charity might dry up. That is a ridiculous position to take; that is all I can say. It is absolutely absurd for a minister to take that position in view of the tremendous responsibility that rests upon the government. Undoubtedly the springs of charity are drying up, but it is not because men are becoming harder hearted. Among the poor at least there never was a time when they were so willing to share what they had with one another. It is not, I say, because the springs of charity in the human heart are drying up but because the resources of the people are becoming so depleted that they cannot give to charity as they have done in the past.
The whole problem has become so vast in its extent .that the ordinary private charities which might handle a few individuals or a few score of individuals in normal times are no longer sufficient to meet what is properly termed a great national emergency. When we remember that anywhere from twenty-five to fifty per cent of the population of a great many of our communities are unemployed, it is ridiculous to think that ordinary private charity can take care of these unfortunate people. It 'cannot be done. Yet the Minister of Trade and Commerce suggested that if the ordinary people of the country should pay a little more attention to this phase of the matter they would solve the problem. Yes; I suppose that if a great drive were put on by the Rotary club a few more men could get work carrying out ashes and doing odd jobs in the way of cleaning up backyards. I had sympathy with that kind of thing five or six years ago when unemployment was relatively a small matter and we thought it would be over in a few weeks. A few odd jobs provided at that time would, it was thought, see the situation through. But it is extraordinary that this government, having been in office for three years and having recognized the necessity for putting on big schemes of public works, and after spending tens of millions of dollars in this way, and with the number of unemployed steadily growing, should come to us now and suggest that we should let the individuals exert themselves a little more. We are further told that we should allow the local community to exert itself more and things .would be looked after better. It does not seem to me that this position is worthy of a government.
Relief Act, 1933

I have not taken very much time in this debate because, frankly, it seems to me that in the last few years I have said everything there was to say again and again; but I cannot let this opportunity go by without once more pleading with the government to take action. It may be that some of us are taking a gloomy view of the matter; it may be that there may not be riots. Undoubtedly there is a great deal of common sense and good judgment among the masses of our people, but I do think that the people have been wonderfully patient during these years. I have often wondered how most of us would behave if for weeks and months and years we had to live as hundreds of thousands of our fellow Canadians have been living. If we do get by without serious riots-and the very fact that the government is taking extraordinary powers would indicate that it is itself not at all sure that we shall-we shall still have to face the very serious deterioration that is taking place in the homes of the hundreds of thousands of people affected. I had word from the part of the country I represent in which someone says, "I can hardly keep from being bitter when I consider the needless suffering and demoralization of the people in this district." Surely we cannot ignore such facts.
People will put up with things for a little time when there is hope for the future; but when they realize that their little earnings are slipping away if they have not already disappeared; when they see their clothing getting shabby and they cannot replace it; when their bedding and household utensils are worn out; when they have not the wherewithal to pay their rent and are months behind; when they see no hope for their children, and there must be thousands whose children, after getting through high school, have nothing to do but roam the streets- when we think of all this, I say the situation becomes wellnigh desperate and we have the right to look to someone for a lead. Yet the minister gets up again and again and says, ''There is the province." But the provinces, as I myself have said so often, and especially the western provinces as everyone knows, are on the verge of bankruptcy and cannot act. Indeed, some of them are bankrupt, just as the municipalities are. Well, what is to be done? We look to the minister to take action, but he shifts ground and says, "We cannot afford it." I urge that so long as there is as much wealth in the dominion as there is to-day, so long as there are large numbers of people drawing enormous revenues from our bonded indebtedness and rMr. Woodswortli.]
from other sources, then we have no right to state that there is no money in Canada to do things. We have no right to say so. If there were war, we could carry on that war and the money would be forthcoming. In his budget speech delivered the other day, the Minister of Finance referred to the great variety of natural resources in this country. He referred also to the resourcefulness of the Canadian people. Our Canadian people are resourceful. They have been so in the past, but the fact is that to-day they have not the opportunities which were to be found in the past. It is not possible for them to do as the pioneers did, and there is no use in our fooling ourselves by going back fifty or seventy-five years and saying -that the people of to-day can fend for themselves just as well as the people of that day. They cannot. The fact remains that to-day they are facing a serious situation.
I am not urging what has sometimes been called direct action; I am not urging violence, *but I must confess that I hardly ever address a meeting either in eastern or western Canada at which the people do not get up afterwards and ask:	What are you going
to do? What can we do about it? When such a question is asked, my mind comes back to this house and to the thought that month after month and year after year we have played this game back and forth and no action has resulted. I confess that I have hardly the courage to continue to speak about these things in the house because of a sense of the futility of it all. Can I go back ' to my friends in my own- constituency in the city of Winnipeg and say to those who have been out of work for several years and who are desperate over it all: " Oh, well, you must wait for another two or three years, there will be an election and perhaps we will put Mr. Bennett and his crowd out and there may be seme improvement in the situation." Is that all we can do? Regardless of what government may be in power or what particular party they may represent, it seems to me that we as the elected representatives of the people have a right to demand that the government should help to solve such a great national problem as unemployment. They turn to us and say:	What alternative
have you to offer or what do you propose? It is not for us to propose the details. We have stated some of the principles on which we believe policies should be based. Both in this country and in the old country the erection of public works has been suggested as a means of increasing the purchasing power of the people. We suggested that here and the government replied:	We cannot

Reliej Act, 1033
afford it. We are supposed to swallow that reply, and the people can continue to suffer. We are told that certain works have been carried on because they could be carried on as relief works where ordinary wages do not have to be paid. Such a course has resulted in the gradual lowering of the standard of living of great sections of our people.
Is not any government elected for the purpose of administering affairs in such a way as to provide a decent living for the people?
I do not want particularly to rub it in, but if ever a government was elected with a mandate to do that, it was this government. After being three years in power we find them receding from their position and simply saying to these poor people:	A lot of you are
malingerers; if the local communities would only get out and rustle, things would go better; you must not load everything upon the state. That is not the way to handle this problem. I do not believe that we can expect that the people will continue much longer to be patient; they should not be patient.	They see their homes going to
pieces and their families degenerating, and yet they know that if there was an efficient government, the situation would be altered.
We are told that we cannot do anything before the world economic conference. All that conference will do will be to pass resolutions and if those resolutions are to mean anything, they will have to be implemented by the people at home. The implementing of these resolutions by Canada would mean a complete reversal of the policy which has been advocated by this government for the last two or three years. Is that likely?
Even at this late stage of the session, I think there should be a reconsideration of this whole matter by the government. We ought not to be asked to go back and tell our people that the government refuses to accept responsibility, that it merely talks about questions of jurisdiction while knowing perfectly well that the provinces and the municipalities are not capable of taking care of the situation. The most unkindest cut of all is when the minister accuses people who are so unfortunate as to be out of work of being malingerers and not desirous of taking a job when they have it placed before them. I do hope that the government will take action even at this late stage.

Mr. Chairman, there is a word or two I should like to say in connection with this problem of unemployment. This problem has two aspects; first, there is the question of giving direct relief to those who find themselves out of work, and, second, there is the matter of deciding what we are
going to do with the number of people who are out of work. The depression first came upon us in the fall of 1929 and since that time the unemployment situation has been gradually going from bad to worse. As I have often said in this house, I do not accuse either the present or the past governments for being entirely responsible for the situation. They were the victims of economic circumstances over which they had no control. But that does not absolve the powers that be from the responsibility of taking care of the situation. The present government has done a great deal to alleviate the sufferings of many people here in Canada. According to the figures submitted by the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gordon), the government has been feeding about one and one-third millions of people in the Dominion of Canada. That is a staggering figure; it gives some idea of the magnitude of the poverty and unemployment which exists in this country.
I think it can be said without fear of contradiction that at this time there are in the neighbourhood of 800,000 people out of work. Figuring each unemployed as representing three persons this gives approximately twenty-five per cent of the population of Canada. I believe the figure is much higher, but if twenty-five per cent of our population is suffering from unemployment, we ought to have some other method of meeting the situation than that of giving relief. The average person, I do not care who he happens to be, would prefer work to being the recipient of direct relief. I think the average person, not only in Canada but in other parts of the world, would prefer to give some service in helping to build up what we might term the state.
The question arises: What are we going to do with these 800,000 people who are out of work? What is going to happen to these people? Let us assume for the sake of argument that conditions will improve in the next six or twelve months, that there is a revival of trade. Even though this does happen, there are hundreds of thousands of men and women who are out of work at the present time who will never be reabsorbed into industry. Hundreds of thosuands of our people are faced with the situation of being permanently out of work. We must find some means of dealing with such a serious situation. A man may be able to stand being out of work for three months, or perhaps six, but ultimately demoralization sets in. Those people who have been unemployed for six, twelve, eighteen months or two years, become unemployable as a result of conditions over which they have
Reliej Act, 1933

no control. I know the minister has taken the question of relief seriously, but what I want him and the government to do is to try to find some means of providing useful work for the hundreds of thousands erf people who are at present unemployed.
The government appointed a commission to investigate the railway problem. Now we are going to -have another commission appointed by the government to investigate the banking situation. Some time ago when I suggested that we might have a commission to investigate the unemployment situation, the government thought that was hardly deserving of consideration. In my opinion the unemployment situation is far more serious than either the banking or the railway problem. Further, I am trying to distinguish between the question of relief and that of a permanent solution of the problem of unemployment. Unless the government can do something in the latter respect, we are building a generation of unemployables and I hate to think what will become of these people in the years to come. Many of these young people who through no fault of their own are unable to secure employment on leaving school at eighteen or twenty years of age and become useful citizens are driven to a life of crime. Our gaols and penitentiaries are filled to overflowing as a result of our unemployment situation. We wish to do away with such a condition, and the only body before which the people of this dominion can place their claims is the federal parliament. When the unemployed in our cities come to the provincial government, the reply is: We have no money. The provincial governments pass the buck to the federal authorities and the federal government in turn says that this is a provincial matter. The unemployment problem is neither municipal nor provincial; it is federal, and if it is a federal problem, it ought to be a federal responsibility. When I speak of its being a federal responsibility, I do so with the idea of dealing not with the question of relief but with the problem of what we are going to do with the vast number who are at present out of work. I know when we come to deal with the more important aspects of the case, we may be told that the federal government has no jurisdiction. But the government has been gathering a vast amount of statistics from the census of 1931 in regard to the wealth and industries of the country.
I feel, as I have stated in the house on many previous occasions, that if we are going to deal with the problem of unemployment- and I want to see it dealt with by the house -we must do away almost entirely with the idea of giving relief to these men and women (Mr. Heaps.]
who are out of work, because I believe by giving them relief, we are in no way even beginning to solve the problem. The only way in which we can do so is by attacking it at its very foundation.
I pointed out . yesterday that within the next few days our two main railways are going to amalgamate certain services. Some hon. members may prefer to call this cooperation, but the first result of this amalgamation of services will be that hundreds, if not thousands, will be thrown out of work. Surely that is no way of dealing with the unemployment problem. If we are to deal with it properly, the first thing we must do is to try to fit in the men who are available to perform useful services in society and to find out what services they can perform. That means making a survey of the whole of the national life of Canada. We have not as yet done that; there has been no attempt to do so, even though we may have a research council. This will mean a great amount of planning by the government, but I think it ought to undertake that planning so that people who have been out of work for years may have some hope; at present they have none.
We have been told in the past few days that we have natural resources, wealth in abundance, all of which is quite true. We have in this country enough wealth, actual and potential, more than to satisfy the needs of the entire population; yet our resources are lying idle and men by the hundreds of thousands are walking the streets who would be only too anxious to render useful service if they were given the opportunity of doing so. I would impress upon the minister, whose heart I know is as big as that of anyone in the house, the need of doing something to deal fundamentally with the hundreds of thousands who are out of work, the main body of whom are and want to be good citizens.
The unemployment problem practically began in 1929 and when it became a little more severe in 1930 some hope was held out that by certain legislation the problem would be solved. But in 1931 it became worse, it was still worse in 1932, and now in 1933, when it is becoming even more acute, very little encouragement is being given to men out of work. About three months ago we were told there were 800.000 people in receipt of relief, and a few weeks ago we were informed that this number had increased to 1,350,000. This gives some indication of the seriousness of the situation with which we are confronted. I hope when we meet after the recess to-night the Minister of Labour will tell the house, the unemployed and the people of Canada

Relief Act, 1933
generally, that the government has a method of dealing with the question that will hold out to our people at present unemployed some hope of having their condition relieved in order that they may become useful citizens.

This brings me to the question of the trans-Canada highway. I am sure that this sum of $3,000,000 will not be sufficient to provide necessary roads in the north, which may affect some of the men placed on the land under the back to the land movement, and there is the other fact that it will be impossible to continue work on the trans-Canada highway. I should like to ask the minister if he would be kind enough to say what is the intention of the federal government with regard to making up the difference between the usual vote of $5,000,000 and the vote this year of $3,000,000 for the northern development branch. The Minister of Labour was most emphatic in his statement with regard to the trans-Canada highway during the last election campaign.

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE YEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext: Surely the hon. member does not mean that not a cent has been spent; surely he knows that many hundreds of thousands of dollars have been spent on what is known as the Ferguson highway. Why, one bridge alone that was built last year cost over $100,000.

speechtext: Quite so.

speechtext:
But I understand there is an agreement between the federal and provincial governments that the cost of the trans-Canada highway is to be divided equally. We have no grudge against any other section of the country, but in the Ottawa valley section, from Mattawa to North Bay, a great deal of employment has been given to a number of young men during the last two years. I have no quarrel with that, but I think the same thing should be done in my part of the country'. I am told also that thousands of men have found employment in the construction of the trans-Canada highway along the north shore of lake Superior. We

maintain that the only logical route for the trans-Canada highway is over the Ferguson highway, and if that route were followed a tremendous amount of money would be saved. I wonder if the minister would be good enough to let me know, if he has the documents before him, what amount of money was spent last year and the year before on the construction of the trans-Canada highway in Ontario.

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE YEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
