speechtext:
I appreciate some of
the information given by the minister, but I cannot allow a personal1 attack upon myself to pass without offering some defence. The minister said that in this house I voted against a certain resolution with respect to the trans-Canada highway. I challenge any 53719-211
member of this house to prove that such a resolution has at any time been introduced in this house while I have been a member. It is true that on one occasion a resolution was brought forward but it had no reference to a trans-Canada highway; there was no mention whatever in that resolution about such a highway. I am referring to the Kellner resolution. The resolution in question was simply one asking the federal government to grant certain sums of money to the provincial government for the building of roads. I repeat, because this is important, that there was no mention either directly or indirectly, of a trans-Canada highway so far as that resolution was concerned. I can assure the minister that had there been any proposal with regard to the trans-Canada highway in that resolution I would have voted for it; I would have raised both hands for it. I do not want Statements of this kind, a statement such as the Minister of Railways also made two years ago, to go unchallenged, for I certainly never did vote against such a resolution. I have always been in favour of that road and I do not think it is fair for the minister to make such a statement. In the year 1926 no resolution was brought forward dealing with the trans-Canada highway or I would certainly have supported it.
May I point out that the Minister of Labour was as strongly in favour of a trans-Canada highway passing through his section of the country when he took part in the last general election; he was for it as much as I have ever been, or as much as my opponent or any Conservative candidate in that part of the country at that time. He cannot get away from that responsibility now. I hope that as a minister he has been using his influence with the cabinet to have the highway routed through that section, but the federal government is now shifting the responsibility on to the provincial government. We have the statement of Mr. Ferguson and Mr. Henry that in the last three years there have been parties of surveyors working west of Hearst and south of lake Nipigon, and it would have been just as easy for those parties during that period to investigate the route through my section as to investigate the route along the north shore of lake Superior and make a definite report.
I am sure the minister wishes to be fair to me and to the house, but I must tell him once more that there never was a measure, introduced in this house which had anything to do with the trans-Canada highway and which I voted against. I challenge any hon. member who has been in this house during the

Relief Act, 1933

last six years to prove that I have ever voted against a proposal of that kind. As regards expenditures voted in connection with the northern development branch, let me say that while I hold no brief for the present Liberal leader in Ontario, I certainly do know that he has never decried any money spent in northern Ontario. He did urge the curtailing of certain governmental expenditures but he never said a word against any moneys spent in connection with the northern development branch. I want to have that also clearly understood, because it is not fair for *the minister to insinuate that it was due to the influence of the present Liberal leader in Ontario that the expenditures for the northern development branch were reduced by $2,000,000.

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE YEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
CONTINUATION FOR ONE YEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext: The reduction is from $5,000,000 to $3,000,000. The vote is now $3,000,000. The minister implies that this reduction came about through the influence of the present Liberal leader in the province.

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE YEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext: I did not mean to imply that.

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE YEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext: Anyone who listened to the hon. gentleman will have inferred just what he meant. I sincerely hope that the minister will find it possible to be as determined in his advocacy of the routing of the trans-Canada highway through that section, now that he is in the cabinet, as he was during the last general election. For my part, I am as much in favour of it to-day as I was ten years ago.

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE YEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext:
I had not intended1 to
discuss this matter until the minister mentioned the Liberal leader in Ontario.

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE YEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext: Which one?

Mr. Mitchell Hepburn,
who will be Prime Minister of Ontario after the next election.

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE YEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext: What will Mr. Sinclair be?

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE YEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext: I have been on the platform with Mr. Hepburn as much as any other man in Ontario and I hope to be with him until we get the Tories cleaned out of the province.

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE YEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext: That will not be long.

speechtext:
I have never heard him
say that he proposed to cut down the expenditures in northern Ontario. The statement

I have heard him make over and over again is this, that he proposes that the money that will be spent in northern Ontario shall be spent in the interests of the people instead of building up a dirty, rotten Tory organization. These are his words and I second the motion. With respect to the highway, I recall that I was in the maritimes when the Prime Minister promised1 a highway to be paid for entirely out of the federal exchequer. More than that, I have in my room a copy of the Halifax Herald, dated between the 10th and the 15th of July, 1930, in which there appears a letter which 'he actually wrote to the people of the maritimes, declaring that if elected on the 28th of July he would begin the immediate construction of a highway to be paid for entirely out of the federal treasury. So that I do not think the minister is doing himself justice in trying now to shift the responsibility to the province.
We all know what difficulties there are in relation to the question of jurisdiction, but I suggest that when a gentleman appears before the public, especially a gentleman aspiring to the office of Prime Minister of Canada, and gives a definite pledge, he ought to keep that pledge; he should regard it as sacred. I recall another thing he said in the maritimes. He said, "I here and now ask every member elected in the maritimes to vote against me in the House of Commons if I do not carry out these pledges."

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE YEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext: How about reforming the Senate?

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE YEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
CONTINUATION FOR ONE YEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext: I venture the opinion that whatever it is, the hon. member blames it upon this government.

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE YEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext: There is no one else but this government to blame. When my hon. friends went through the country in 1930 there were 117,000 unemployed and they claimed that that unemployment existed because of the fiscal policies of the Liberal party. The number of unemployed to-day is nearer to 800,000 than it is to 100,000.

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE YEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext: How about giving up your engine ?

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE YEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext:
If my hon. friend is
ashamed to put on overalls, I am not.
What did my hon. friends promise during the last elections? They said that if they were elected they would end unemployment or perish in the attempt. The boys and girls are back home, but what are we going to do for them? Are we going to send them up into the northern Ontario camps and pay them S5 per month and their board?

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE YEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext: Carried.

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE YEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext: That is about the only thing a Tory can do, cast ridicule upon the unemployed and their misery.

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE YEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext: Rot.

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE YEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext:
I never knew a Tory that did it.
53719-211J

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE YEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext: They put into effect tariff policies which cut the trade of this country by more than fifty per cent, they throw thousands of railway men out of work and then offer a policy of unemployment relief. When one of us on this side refers to the misery which exists in his own particular riding, he gets nothing but the usual "ha! ha! " from the Tory ranks. Mr. Chairman, I suggest that if some of the hon. members to your right would prefer to laugh and snort and sneer, they would be better in the smoking room where they belong. Last night we asked some civil questions of the minister and after a great deal of trouble we obtained some of the information we required but not all.

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE YEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext:
They ought to be
intelligent questions.

speechtext:
When we mentioned unemployment insurance the minister did something which I did not think any minister of the crown would attempt to do. former minister said with regard to unemployment." I have files in my office which will show that the former government petitioned or canvassed the provinces in connection with a scheme for unemployment insurance. This file shows also that some of the provinces were willing to join any federal scheme in this connection. It does not do the minister any good to adopt such tactics. Whether I am in or out of this house, I do not intend that the Minister of Labour or any hon. member on the other side shall misrepresent the position taken by myself or by the government of which I was a member.

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE YEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext: In or out, it will not make any difference.

speechtext: You are the first; start it.

speechtext: I say to the hon. member; it won't be long now.

why not go now?

speechtext: Not a five cent piece.

I advise my hon. friends who are sneering and laughing to call another convention to meet in the city of Winnipeg and change tiheir name from the Liberal-Conservative association to the hard time party of Canada. I recall a member of the government standing up in 1921 and saying: "Mr. Speaker, why have we unemployment in this country? subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE YEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext:

thing.

We ought to have the required information from the minister. We ought to know whether or not the government are going to build the trans-Canada highway, which the Prime Minister promised to do, not only in his speeches but in letters written to the newspapers. As under section 2 there is provision for making agreements with the provinces, I should like to ask the minister this question: Will the agreement contemplate that private organizations shall disburse money and then be reimbursed by the province and the dominion? -and to pass for payment the accounts for the dominion contribution to the expenditures reported by the provinces as having been made by the municipality, including in such municipal expenditures amounts voluntarily contributed by individuals, business firms, or associations, to the municipality, providing that such amounts have been utilized solely for relief purposes, and have been expended under the jurisdiction of the municipal authorities, and provided that such funds have not been raised by arbitrary deductions from wages payable to those engaged on relief work.

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE YEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932

Upon such terms and conditions as may be agreed upon,-enter into agreements with any of the provinces respecting relief measures therein; grant financial assistance to any province by way of loan, advance, guarantee or otherwise; loan or advance money to or guarantee the payment of money by any public body, corporation or undertaking.

speechtext: I am afraid I do not just follow the hon. member.

speechtext: In many countries there are similar schemes whereby the government contributes through the labour unions. When I saw that order in council, it gave me encouragement to think the minister might adopt the scheme in a more general way instead of just through one particular organization.

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE YEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext: I know some of the organizations that have been in receipt of the grants just mentioned and I know they have been doing very good work for the money received. speechtext: I have not the information before me. There have not been many such organizations. speechtext: If I understood the minister correctly, the government have no objection to such services being given by private organizations under the jurisdiction of the local authorities?

speechtext:
We have an organization in the municipality of Burnaby named the Army of Common Good, eight or nine hundred strong, composed of people who have gone out to

help themselves, and I do not suppose there is a finer organization in the whole of Canada. They have gone out cultivated vacant parcels of ground, cut wood, et cetera, which they sell for firewood. speechtext:
I have no knowledge of
its having been done; in fact I am sure it has not been done in any instance. The only exception in the past under the other relief act was the first advance of about $1,400,000 to the Canadian Pacific Railway Company and then the $1,000,000 which has been authorized but not yet paid.

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE YEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext:
Has the minister any
knowledge, or can he deny, that advances have been made by a province to industrial firms to subsidize pay-rolls?

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE YEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext:
I am not in a position
to state whether or not a province has done that, but I know we have not contributed to it.

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE YEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext:
I would submit to the
minister that subsidizing the pay-roll of an
industry in order to relieve unemployment within a municipality might have very far-reaching and disastrous effects on competition in another province. Inasmuch as it has been suggested-I can find no proof of it; nevertheless it causes some anxiety-that in some cases the provincial government has actually subsidized the pay-roll of an industry in order to keep men employed rather than have them go on relief, it seems to me the minister should have some control over a practice of that kind. If not, he is putting industry in other provinces at a very unfair disadvantage compared with the industry to which such treatment is given.

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE YEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext: I think I can assure the members of the committee that this government would not be a party, and certainly has not been in the past, to any contribution for the purpose suggested. I can readily see that it would result in exactly what the hon. member has pointed out.

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE YEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext: If such a practice were indulged in by one province, would the minister's department necessarily know about it, and has he any check upon it?

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE YEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext: We would not know unless we were asked to contribute. But if application were made to the government to contribute we would immediately inquire into all the ramifications of that industry, and I can assure the committee that this government would not make a contribution that would result in the situation suggested by the hon. member for North Bruce (Mr. Malcolm). Of course we do in effect subsidize some industries in this country, like the coal industry, but that is covered by legislation.

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE YEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext: That is statutory; we understand it.

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE YEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext: I have no objection to the statutory subsidy to which the minister refers. But I would like to ask the minister if he can secure information from the provinces as to whether or not they have through their own treasuries subsidized the pay-rolls of any industry.

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE YEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext: I am afraid I will have to answer by saying that I have enough trouble on my hands without going on a prospecting trip to find what the provinces are doing.

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE YEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext:
Following that a step further, may I ask whether, if the provinces did enter upon that practice of subsidizing industries, it necessarily follows that they specify all the
Relief Act, 1933

expenditures they make when they apply to the federal government for its share of the cost? Does the dominion know exactly what the money is being expended for?

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE YEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext:
Yes. The department
knows what the money is being devoted to. The information that accompanies the certificate of expenditure from the province discloses the purpose for which the money is asked. And of course the Auditor General again checks the expenditure to see that it falls within the agreement and the statute. This part of the legislation referring to corporations I can well understand must be given the most careful attention, and it would be with great reluctance that advances would be made to public corporations, such as the advance to the wage earners on the Canadian Pacific Railway. It would have to be a very special case. The danger that has been pointed out by the hon. member for North Bruce would be one of the first questions that would have to be looked into, because undoubtedly if such a practice were adopted, in even one instance, it might easily result in very unfair competition, and dislocation of industry, which would be regrettable, and for which, of course, this government would be held directly responsible.

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE YEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext: I am very glad the minister has made that statement. Inasmuch as this relief money is voted jointly by the federal and the provincial governments, there should be some understanding between the federal and provincial authorities that such a practice shall not obtain. The fact that one province might subsidize an industry within its borders by granting it so much money towards its pay-roll would simply mean that that industry would be enabled to cut prices to the disadvantage of like industries in other provinces. It is a practice from which no good could come, but only strife, both for the wage earners and the manufacturers in other provinces. As the federal and provincial governments are carrying on this relief work jointly, I think the minister should have an understanding that no such unfair practice can possibly be allowed in the future, even though it may not have taken place in the past. I base my remarks on rumours that are current that such a practice has obtained. I do not confirm them; I know nothing of their truth, nevertheless such rumours are current.

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE YEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext:
Although a great many figures have been quoted by the minister in this debate, it is difficult to find from those

figures the amount that has been advanced to the different provinces under all the different schemes. I know that the minister has been very patient and has given a great many figures, but I defy anyone to find out what has been contributed to any one province under all these different heads. If the minister has not the information here to-night I shall be glad to put my question on the order paper, but I think we should have, in percentage to population, the full amount contributed under the different schemes in the different provinces.

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE YEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext:

by the hon. member was given to the house by me on February 24 of this year. subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE YEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext:
I should be very pleased
to have it in any form at all, because I believe we should have the per capita figures for the different provinces, and I do not think any percentages according to population have been given.

speechtext:

speechtext: Certainly.

speechtext:
I think that could be
worked out easily. The hon. member means the per capita expenditure under each item indicated?

speechtext:
Quite so.
Mr. GORDON; I will have a schedule worked' out and furnished to the hon. gentleman.

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE YEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext:
In connection with section
2, which provides that notwithstanding the provisions of any statute or law the governor in council may loan or advance money to or guarantee the payment of money by any public body, corporation or undertaking, may I ask the minister if any such loans or advances or guarantees have been made to private corporations or to undertakings, whatever that may mean, since January 1, 1932, except the advance made to the Canadian Pacific Railway?

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE YEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext:
As has been indicated
already, there was a payment made to the Canadian Pacific Railway. There was also a guarantee given which has been referred to and explained in the house in connection with the Manitoba savings office. So far as my recollection serves me, no other guarantees or advances have been made to corporations.
I think my recollection is correct in that.

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE YEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext:
Then may I ask the minister if the government is committed to any other guarantees, and I use the word "committed advisedly. I intend to come back to this under section 7, because on reading over certain orders in council which have been produced I find that with reference to the first Canadian Pacific loan of $1,147,221.71 the government entered into an agreement with that company under the terms of which the Canadian Pacific was to keep its shops open from the 17th day of November, 1931, until the 31st day of December, 1931. Parliament was in session, I think, from about February 10, 1932, until well into the month of June, if. my memory serves me aright, and during all that time we were not informed of this agreement between the administration and the Canadian Pacific. As a matter of fact the order in council was passed only on September 30, 1932, whereas the agreement or guarantee was given almost a year before, and the money was actually expended. I submit that it is bad enough to have the government take all the powers given to it under this act, by means of which parliament is absolutely ignored and the government is permitted, notwithstanding the provisions of any statute or law, to do anything they think should be done; at least there is some kind of implied obligation to tell this house what has been done, and I submit that arrangements made verbally or over the long distance telephone between the minister and any corporation at once should be put in writing and placed before parliament. It is useless for us to have in this act section 7 which says:
All orders in council and regulations made under the provisions of this act shall be laid before the House of Commons forthwith after the making thereof if parliament is then sitting, or if not, said orders in council or regulations or an abstract thereof disclosing their essential provisions shall be published in the next following issue of the Canada Gazette.
We may as well remove that section if the government can deal in millions of dollars without informing parliament. As a matter of fact I am informed that in the Beauharnois case it was months after the arrangement was made to guarantee the bonds that anything was placed in writing; everything was done by telephone. I have great respect for all the members of the government and for the Prime Minister but I submit that it is not fair to the contracting parties or to the government that at least some memorandum binding the government should not be made. No private business in the world would be carried on in that way, particularly when dealing with millions of dollars.
While I am on my feet I might as well refer to another order in council dealing with wheat, which I think I have in my desk. In the very preamble of the first order in council, dated November 15, 1932, providing for the guarantee to the banks to cover the gambling operations of the wheat pool, it is stated:
The committee of the privy council have had before them a report, dated llith September, 1931, from the Minister of Finance, recommending that, in pursuance of the Unemployment and Farm Relief Act, 1931, and of an undertaking on behalf of the government, made before the session of parliament at which said act was passed, to implement by legislation the recommendation hereinafter set out, the governor in council guarantee repayment to the chartered banks hereinafter mentioned:
The reason I asked the minister if anything had been ddne by way of a commitment is that we might be sitting here, and in fact we were sitting here, for months without being informed of undertakings, obligations, guarantees or contracts made by the government. So I say the section in question is absolutely useless; we might as well take it out of the act altogether unless we add something making it apply when agreements are made or decisions arrived at or legislation passed, because each order in council has the force and effect of an act of this house. Unless we have some assurance from the government that some such action will be taken I believe this section of the act might just as well be taken out. Having given the minister my reasons for the question, I now ask whether the government is committed in any way to
Relief Act, 1933

any private corporation, to any province or to any private person for the expenditure of money or the guaranteeing of any expenditure of money in any way other than in the orders in council which have been produced in this house within the last few months.

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE YEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext: I do not believe that any guarantees have been made under this part of the section other than the ones with which the committee has dealt, namely, to the Canadian Pacific Railway, the guarantee against loss in connection with Beauharnois- I am not sure whether that was dealt with under the Relief Act-

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE YEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext: Yes, it was.

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE YEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext: -that with respect to the wheat pools, and the Manitoba savings office; and the Dominion government is not obligated to any provincial government, corporation or individual in connection with any guarantee under the provisions of the act still in force. With respect to the Canadian Pacific Railway and the fact that the assurance was given in the fall of 1931, and the order in council was not in fact passed until the following year, the circumstances in connection with this matter were explained by the Prime Minister. The situation was this. The Canadian Pacific Railway approached the Dominion government and outlined the difficulties which they were in, and the government was also approached by the head of the labour unions. After the matter had received consideration the assurance was given in the fall of 1931 that, for the period of time indicated by the hon. member, the advance would be made to the Canadian Pacific Railway to pay the wages of these men, and of course the advance would be made only after the wages had been earned. Proof of the payment of the wages was not received by the government until the following year, and of course the order in council was not passed until the proof that the wages had been paid and that the men had been employed was furnished to the government. That is the reason the order in council was delayed after the assurance had been given in the fall. That was the situation with respeot to the Canadian Pacific Railway guarantee.

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE YEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext: I understand there were two loans to the Canadian Pacific Railway.

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE YEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext:
The first was a guarantee of wages of SI.400.000 odd, and there was authorization of a further $1,000,000 to be paid
fMr. Power.]
to the Canadian Pacific Railway when the wages were earned. That money has not yet been paid.

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE YEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext: The loan has really been made in two parts. I believe the first loan was made without interest, and it was not to be repaid until such time as the railway again paid in excess of five per cent in dividends. Was the second loan made under the same terms and conditions, and if not what were the terms and conditions?

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE YEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext: There were two orders in council. The first one dealt with a loan of $1,447,222.71 and was a loan to the Canadian Pacific Railway repayable without interest when the earnings of the company enabled it to resume payments of dividends at not more than five per cent per annum. The second, passed on December 22, 1932, is to be paid back to the government without interest before any further dividends on any stock of the Canadian Pacific Railway are declared or paid.

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE YEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext:
Listening to the ex-Minister of Labour, I was astounded when he made the statement that this government had advanced a certain amount of money to the Navy League of Ontario. Before dealing with that matter, however, there is a more pleasing duty to perform, Mr. Chairman (Mr. Spotton) and that is to wish you, sir, many happy returns of the day, and may your shadow never grow less. I preface my remarks with that compliment so that you will not call me to order in the course of what I have to say.
I can understand that under this subsection (a) of section 2 of the bill before us, very wide powers are given, and it seems that under this clause almost any person can ask the provincial or the federal government for money and get it.

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE YEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext: Glad to hear it.

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE YEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext:
My hon. friend gets some wisdom listening to me. lit seems to me that "Navy League of Ontario" is rather a misnomer; I do not understand how that body can apply to this government or to the provincial government for relief. I could understand, so far as the province of Ontario is concerned, that there might be an application from the egg circle of West York, if it spent money for relief purposes and wanted assistance from the province or the dominion, or an application from the potato growers' association of Lambton county, or from the organization known as the Grange, or even from

Relief Act, 1933
the Ku Klux Klan or the Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals. I could understand it if the application came from any of these organizations. It seems to me however that there is something wrong in the distribution of relief by this government and the province when they allow an organization known as the Navy League of Ontario to distribute moneys and expect the taxpayers to pay for it. Again, I could understand that from any of the cities of Vancouver, Halifax, Montreal and Quebec an application might come and the navy league in any of these places might have something to do with the distribution of relief, under agreement with this government or with the province interested. But if the yachtsmen of Toronto and places on lake Ontario want to put crn a little swank and, instead of calling their organization the yacht club of Toronto, they decide to call it the Navy League of Ontario, that is no good reason why the federal or the provincial government should allow them to spend money and then ask the taxpayers of the country to foot the bill. If that is the way the money is being distributed, then it is high time a halt was called. I should like to have a detailed statement from the minister in connection with the $2,174.12 which was distributed by the navy league under order in council passed on June 20, 1932. I realize there are certain organizations which are doing good work in the distribution of relief money but it seems to me that it is going too far when an organization on lake Ontario or in the city of Toronto known as the navy league is permitted to distribute money. I should like to know how this money was distributed and who received it.

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE YEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext: A Lunenburg navy would be much better, wouldn't it?

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE YEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext: Yes, much better.

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE YEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext: The money was not paid by this government to the Ontario navy league; it was disbursed by the navy league and the province of Ontario paid a portion of the cost while the Dominion government contributed its percentage. I have not before me the details of the actual expenditures and the names of the persons to whom relief was granted, but if it is not in the department I am sure it can be obtained from the Ontario government. I shall obtain it and give it to the hon. member, if he so desires.

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE YEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext:
Do I understand that when the government receives a request from an organization like this navy league of Toronto it
pays the money out without knowing what it is to be used for, who is to receive it and so on? I can understand that in a city like Toronto there must be many people who are receiving relief, but surely the different churches, the different labour unions and other organizations are better qualified to do this work than a little two by four, freshwater organization which comes and asks for money from the dominion treasury.

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE YEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext: Oh, oh.

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE YEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext: Although my hon. friends may laugh, I am serious about this. There must be something loose in the organization looking after this relief when a so-called organization known as the navy league must step into the breach in the great province of Ontario and the great city of Toronto. There must be hundreds of organizations looking after relief in that city, and I do not think the government should countenance an organization like the navy league coming in and getting money from this dominion. I hope the minister will note my remarks and will see that relief is given through sources other than the navy league.

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE YEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext:
I should
like to refer to the latter part of subsection (a) of section 2 of this bill and ask the minister if I am right in assuming that from now on no notes will be taken from people in the province of Saskatchewan who are recipients of relief.

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE YEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext:
The taking of notes in
the province of Saskatchewan has been the subject of discussion upon a number of occasions. I believe it is clear in the minds of hon. members that these notes were taken because the people themselves did not want charity. I assume there were some who in their extremity were not very anxious to repay, but a great number of the people did want to pay back and are paying back. Therefore, the Saskatchewan relief commission took notes from them all. Our future course will have to depend upon the situation existing in each individual instance. It is remotely possible that a situation may arise similar to that which arose in Saskatchewan where the people were destitute because of the total failure of their crops. Those people were not without assets but the assets they had could not be converted into money. I would not care to give the assurance that in a similar instance a similar course would not be adopted. I am sure the hon. member will recognize that many of the people in the
Relief Act, 1933

dried out areas of Saskatchewan have an earnest desire to pay back the amounts advanced to them. As the statement which I spread upon the records discloses, they are paying them back.

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE YEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext:
There
are a great many people throughout the province of Saskatchewan who, like myself, have wondered just why it was 'that the recipients of relief in that province were called upon to give notes for the relief they received. We have been wondering this because of the statement made by the Prime Minister on July 29, 1931. At that time the Prime Minister said:
During the last few days I have received telegrams from the province of Saskatchewan suggesting that it was not desirable that direct relief which might be regarded as charity should be accorded to those hardy settlers who have lost their all for the third, and in some instances the fourth succeeding year, but rather that they would like to execute some document which would indicate that they regarded the help given as an obligation which they might sometime be able to pay. I would say to my good friend from South Huron (Mr. McMillan) that that indicates at least the attitude of most of those who at the present time are without crops and who have had the third succeeding crop failure.
In view of that statement, I asked for a return of all the correspondence which had been received from people in the province of Saskatchewan in connection with the giving of notes by farmers in that district. My request was placed upon the order paper early in the session of 1932 and was passed by the house on March 23, 1932. On May 4 the return had not come down and I asked why it had not been brought down. At that time the Prime Minister said that he thought it had been brought down. I made an inquiry some weeks after and I was then told it would be brought down before the end of the session. On May 23, the Prime Minister made this statement:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. McKenzie) has asked me a question on several occasions. I thought he had misread what I said on the 29th July, 1931, I find on looking up the record that I then said:
"During the last few days I have received telegrams from the province of Saskatchewan suggesting that it was not desirable that direct relief which might be regarded as charity should be accorded to those hardy settlers who have lost their all for the third, and in some instances the fourth succeeding year, but rather that they would like to execute some document which would indicate that they regarded the help given as an obligation which they might sometime be able to pay. I would say to my good friend from South Huron (Mr. McMillan) that that indicates at least the attitude of most 
of those who at the present time are without crops and who have had the third succeeding crop failure."
I observe the hon. gentleman read my remarks as indicating that I had received communications from the province of Saskatchewan, and he was seeking information as to what member of the provincial government had communicated with me. It will be observed that my language did not mean that I had received communications from the provincial government, but from persons residing within the province. While some of the communications were marked "personal," the one that gave me the most information was from a loan company manager, who, I knew, had travelled over the territory and found a disposition on the part of the settlers not to take charity but to make a contribution in the sense indicated.
That was not by any means a satisfactory reply. I never at any time indicated that I thought the communication came from a member of the provincial government; that was not in my mind at all. But people in Saskatchewan are still asking who it was that was so much concerned about the business as to telegraph to the Prime Minister that they should be allowed to give notes for the relief they received. We are still wondering who it was, and I think, in fairness to the many other managers of loan companies in Saskatchewan, the Prime Minister should tell us who this particular gentleman was who knows so much about the farmers. I have discussed the matter with many farmers and they say that they would like to know who it was, because they are sure that no farmer in Saskatchewan requested permission to give a note for the relief he received. If there are any such farmers, we would like to know who they are and who this loan manager was. We would like to know who it was that was so busy as to send these requests to the Prime Minister that the farmers dhould give notes for their relief. Can we have an answer to this?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE YEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman knows quite well it would be impossible for me to make any statement as to names,^although my memory is fairly good. I looked up the matter at the time and gave an answer before the end of last session for the very reason that the hon. gentleman asked for the information and I endeavoured to supply it. The telegrams were marked "personal." The gentleman was a manager of a loan company who had just completed travelling over the territory. I had stopped at Regina and discussed the matter at that time. When we were sitting around the table it was said that a number of the farmers desired to give notes, and as a matter of fact the commission did prepare notes which were signed by those who received relief.

That a number of farmers would ask about the matter seems passing strange in view of Ihe fact that they gave notes in large numbers. All that received relief gave notes for the relief they got and I did not think anything more about the matter. The hon. gentleman asked for the correspondence. Perhaps he is not aware that between August 7, 1931 and February of 1932, according to the file clerks, as many file boxes were filled as during the term of office of my predecessor, so it is a little difficult to carry all these things in mind. I did at the time endeavour to give an answer to the hon. gentleman. I do not now recall the name of the gentleman, but he said that he had just completed a tour and his statement only confirmed what had been told ro me at the meeting held in Regina where we were all sitting round the board together and discussing these matters. While we did not arrange the notes, they were given by the farmers and I understood, although not until after my explanation in the house, that they were taken in favour of the crown in right of the dominion, which wras not our understanding of the matter at the time. That, however, was done. The Premier of Saskatchewan was reported as saying that some $400,000 had been returned of loans that had been made for relief purposes. That was with respect to seed, as I understand the matter. That the farmers gave notes, there is no doubt in the world. That they agreed to give notes, was, as I understood the situation, a matter of arrangement. From what was said to me at the time of my visit to Regina as well as from the communications to which I referred when I looked them up something like a year ago now, it will be apparent that the farmers who were receiving relief desired to return it. Moreover, I received many communications stating that it was highly desirable that that should be done, because nothing was worse than that relief should be distributed without any idea of its ever being repaid. A number of citizens speaking from an organization standpoint said that if we desired to prevent the evil consequences that might flow from giving direct relief, every man who received it should sign for it, indicating not only the receipt of it but a willingness to repay it if he ever were in a position to do so.

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE YEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext:
I think the farmers were not averse to giving notes for the seed grain that they received, but they feel there was an injustice because they were compelled to sign for every pound of tea and everything else they got and give a note for them, whereas in the cities that was not done
Relief Act, 1933
until very much later. It looks as if the farmers were not given a square deal in having to sign notes for everything they got in the way of relief.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE YEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext:
It is only well that the hon. member should bear in mind that the provinces had control of the distribution of relief in the cities and that the dominion undertook full responsibility only with respect to those seventy odd municipalities in which there had been a complete loss of crop for three succeeding years. Even then a commission was appointed by the province at the request of the Dominion government, and the Dominion government dealt with the province.
I might say to the hon. member for Antigo-nish-Guysborough that there was no dealing with any navy league or any other organization by the Dominion government; it dealt only with the provinces and the provinces made the arrangements, because, as I read the constitution-and I may be entirely in error-the dominion does not deal with organizations or communities except through the province. The province alone is the medium of communication and contact between those who receive relief and the Dominion government.

subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE YEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext: But the fact remains that this government and the people generally had to pay this money which, as the Prime Minister said, was paid out under the arrangement made by the province with the navy league. When that request to pay this money came in from the province, the federal government should have turned down the request and not paid the money. There are navy leagues in different parts of the country and their officials go out and collect private subscriptions to look after sailors who are not able to take care of themselves. I object to the federal government paying this money. It seems to me that if other sums are paid by the government in the same way, it is time we had a royal commission to investigate the matter.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: CONTINUATION FOR ONE YEAR OF PROVISIONS OF RELIEF ACT, 1932
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman,
despite his prejudice, does not desire to be unfair. May I say to him that the province of Ontario selected the navy league as an instrument to distribute relief amounting in the aggregate to $2,000. As I have said, we know of the difficulties of foreseeing in a world such as this what will happen within twenty-four hours. We know that tonight in some great cities with populations as great as this there is but one bank functioning. These things could not have been foreseen by any human judgment a month ago. Weighing the advantages and disadvantages with the best judgment we have and applying the principle which I fancy has governed all governments desiring to do what is best for their own populations consistent with their obligations, contractual and otherwise, we have arrived at the conclusion I have indicated. We thought it desirable that these matters should be mentioned in this way in order that we might make known to the house everything upon which we believe that action should be taken. That does not indicate in any sense that conditions will not arise which may necessitate in the very nature of things action of a like character being taken in connection with other matters not now mentioned.
Will any provision be made in regard to the stabilization fund to ensure that the producer derives the benefit rather than the exporter?

I listened with some
interest to the observations of the Prime Minister in the course of which he stated that the relief granted by paying the difference between the existing rate of exchange on the pound sterling and $4.60 was to be treated as a relief measure. It strikes me that the very limitation of the list which the Minister of Finance gave in his budget condemns the scheme entirely. I quite appreciate the fact that had Canada followed the course of Australia and gone off the gold standard with Great Britain so that the dollar would be on a parity with the pound, Canadian agriculture would not be at the disadvantage it is with regard to the export of dairy produce or of wool, a commodity which was promised all sorts of protection by my hon. friends opposite and which is not to have even the advantage of the assistance of the difference in exchange. The question was asked a moment ago by somebody as to what this would cost. The minister did not seem to be able to give a very definite answer. Has the order in council been passed extending the benefits of the agricultural stabilization fund to the thirteen products?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: No.
Is it anticipated that it will be passed in the near future?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: That depends upon the action of the house.
The government has power, under the present relief legislation, to pass it, has it not?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Inasmuch as the present act expires on March 31 of this year, it is hoped that this bill may be enacted before that date. If it is, then we would have the power.
But the government has it under the present act?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
We have not done it
under the present act.
The same clause is in the present legislation?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Yes, there is no change in that. The power is there, but as the present act expires on March 31 and this is the 23rd, eight days from now the act would expire and it is hardly desirable to pass an order in council in respect to stabilization fund for that short time.
Would the order in council expire the moment the act did?

If there arise in other industries conditions that make it advisable in the opinion of the government to extend to them similar relief, would other orders in council be passed from time to time covering other commodities than the thirteen mentioned by the Minister of Finance on Tuesday last?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I was trying to say to the committee that the government did reserve to itself the power to deal with a situation as it might arise, but that as regards a relief measure it was thought desirable that the house should be made acquainted with the view of the government with respect to those commodities mentioned as being the ones which the government felt, with the best information at its disposal, were entitled to the benefit of such relief.

There was one question asked the Prime Minister and I do not know whether he heard it, but it seems important: it was Whether the government had provided any means or guarantee whereby the 'benefit of the proceeds of this agricultural stabilization fund will go to the producers and not to the exporters?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
It is obvious that the
benefits will first of all accrue normally to the importer, whose invoices will be the determining factor with respect to the matter, but unless the benefits are reflected in better prices for the producer, we realize we shall not have accomplished the object we desire to attain. Under the legislation now under consideration there will be ample power in the government to deal with that situation; but I think it is clear we did succeed in seeing that the benefits in connection with the bonus on wheat went directly to the producer.
Not on canned fruit.
Or canned fish.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman may be able to speak with authority on the subject, but we believe the benefits can be made appreciable to the producer, and that is the object of this legislation. When we have endeavoured with all our power, such as it is, to bring the benefit to the producer, we have usually managed to succeed.
Progress reported.
